snippet.title: Why Falling Elevators Don't Stop Instantly
snippet.description:
If an elevator cable snaps, why don't safety brakes lock the car instantly?

In 1854, Elisha Otis demonstrated the instant catch: cut the rope, throw teeth into the guide rails, and freeze the platform in place. But inside a modern high-speed elevator, an instant stop would subject passengers to over 10G of deceleration force—causing severe skeletal trauma and internal injury.

Modern elevator safety brakes are deliberately designed to do the opposite: they are built to slip.

In this breakdown, we explore the purely mechanical systems operating inside elevator shafts:
• The Overspeed Governor: How a zero-power flyball mechanism trips at 115% rated speed without computers or electricity.
• Progressive Safety Wedges: Why falling cars pull their own brake levers into narrowing tapered slots.
• Disc Spring Packs: The calibrated metal flex that lets the brake jaws bite and scrape the steel guide rails over 0.5 to 1.0 meter.
• The Upward Runaway Paradox: What happens when an empty car is pulled upward by a heavy counterweight, bypassing standard downward safety wedges.

Standards & Regulatory Citations Referenced:
- EN 81-20 / EN 81-50 (European Elevator Safety Rules)
- ASME A17.1 / CSA B44 (Safety Code for Elevators and Escalators)
